summary: This Investopedia-style article defines foreign debt (external debt) as money borrowed by governments, corporations or households from foreign governments, private lenders, or international organizations such as the World Bank, ADB and IMF. It explains why borrowers take on foreign debt, how it is tracked, and how excessive levels can slow growth, trigger debt crises, and contribute to human-rights problems. The article also notes that low interest rates since 2008 and the coronavirus downturn raise the likelihood of future debt crises.
one_line: Explains foreign (external) debt: its definition, reasons countries borrow abroad, economic and human costs, and links to crises.
key_facts: Foreign debt is money borrowed by a government, corporation or private household from another country's government or private lenders.
Foreign debt also includes obligations to international organizations such as the World Bank, Asian Development Bank (ADB), and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Foreign debt is also known as external debt and has been rising steadily in recent decades.
For low-income countries especially, borrowing from international organizations like the World Bank is an essential option, offering funding at attractive rates and with flexible repayment schedules.
Local debt markets may not be deep enough to meet borrowing needs, particularly in developing countries, which is one reason governments borrow abroad.
The World Bank, with the IMF and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), gathers short-term foreign debt data from the Quarterly External Debt Statistics (QEDS) database.
Excessive foreign debt can hamper countries' ability to invest in infrastructure, education, or health care, because limited revenue goes to servicing loans.
Foreign debt is usually denominated in the currency of the lender's country, so if the borrowing country's currency weakens, its debts become harder to service.
High levels of foreign debt contributed to the Asian Financial Crisis and, at least in the case of Greece and Portugal, the Eurozone debt crisis.
According to one estimate, the amount developing country governments paid toward foreign debt nearly doubled from 2010 to 2018, as a percentage of government revenues.
Extraordinarily low interest rates since the 2008 Global Financial Crisis made it easier for governments, businesses, and consumers to take on higher levels of debt.
The article says a disruptive debt crisis in one or more countries seems likely in the not-too-distant future, given the severe global downturn from the novel coronavirus.
The United Nations has linked high levels of foreign debt and dependency on foreign assistance to human rights abuses, since economic distress causes governments to cut social spending.
